Hitscan beats it: the heavy cannon, or the plasma rifle's microwave beam, which holds it in place for a few seconds even after you stop firing, long enough for a quick weapon-swap combo. An ice bomb is the other answer, freezing it mid-slither. Do not meathook it; it answers with an energy wave that knocks you off the hook.

sections.name: Arch-vile
sections.card: A walking buff totem: while it lives everything in the arena hits harder and moves faster, glowing red, and it summons more demons, drawn from that fight's list and sometimes as bad as tyrants or marauders. It summons while you are locked into a glory kill or chainsaw animation, because you cannot interrupt it then, and its new arrivals stand in an orange aura, frozen and undamageable, until it finishes. So find it first, skip the executions until it is dead, and put your heaviest ordnance into it. Its magic shield ignores plasma, and it counts as super heavy, so no chainsaw.

sections.name: Super Shotgun and meat hook
sections.card: Picked up in the Cultist Base and never put down: massive point-blank damage, several fodder demons per shot, a pinky in one shot to the tail, but a long reload and nothing at range. The reload disappears if you swap to another gun and back. The meathook under the barrel is the movement tool: fire it into a demon and it yanks you to them for the blast, or across the arena for the escape. Small enemies are held in place when hooked; big ones are not, and may hit you on the way in, so be ready to jump off. It will not grab a marauder or riot shield facing you, nor the gladiator behind its shield, and a knockback hit or a dash lets go.

sections.name: The Crucible
sections.card: A sword that kills any demon in one swing without a stagger, marauders excepted (they must be stunned first), and the Doom hunter, which costs two: one for the sled, one for the body. It holds three charges, refilled only at fixed spots in the level, and one swing spends one charge whether it lands on a tyrant or an imp, so treat every charge as a tyrant. Each kill returns health. Save it for the super heavies in the last arenas and for the Icon fight, where the charges and blood punches on its summons are how you stay alive.

sections.name: Slayer Gates, keys and the Fortress
sections.card: The purple gore nests behind locked gates are optional arenas harder than anything around them; each opens with a Slayer Key hidden nearby, in Exultia, Cultist Base, Super Gore Nest, ARC Complex, Mars Core and Taras Nabad. Clearing one pays three weapon points and an Empyrean Key, and all six keys unlock the Unmaykr in the Fortress, a rapid three-orb gun that shares the BFG's ammo. Back at the Fortress, Sentinel batteries from the levels open doors two at a time for crystals, mod bots, suit points and skins, and the twelve Sentinel crystals in blue shrines raise health, armour or ammo four steps each. The flame belch, ice bomb and ballista are collected there between missions.

sections.name: Starting out in Doom 64
sections.card: Not a port: a separate sequel to Doom II with thirty-two new levels, redrawn larger sprites, coloured lighting and a slower, darker mood. The whole Doom II arsenal is here plus one new gun, the Unmaker, and most of the classic monsters, but no arch-viles, revenants, spider mastermind or chaingunners; the new faces are the fast, half-invisible nightmare imp and the Mother Demon at the end. Four secret levels hide the game's real reward, and the 2020 re-release adds a further episode, The Lost Levels, after the ending. Play it like classic Doom: find keys, hit switches, and treat every quiet room as a trap.

sections.name: Nightmare imp
sections.card: The first new monster you meet: a translucent blue-purple imp, twice as fast as the ordinary kind, throwing purple fireballs that fly twice as fast too, and hard to see against dark walls. Treat every dim doorway as holding one. It is still an imp in health, so the shotgun handles it; the danger is the pack and the speed, not the toughness. First seen in Main Engineering, and there are a lot of them.

sections.name: Unmaker and the Demon Keys
sections.card: The one new gun: a demonic laser that eats cells, found first in the secret level Outpost Omega and not again until Altar of Pain. On its own it is a slower, stronger plasma gun. Each of the three Demon Keys, one hidden on each of the secret levels Outpost Omega, The Lair and In The Void, powers it up: faster firing, then a second beam, then a third, until it fires so fast that it stun-locks anything in the game, the Cyberdemon and the Mother Demon included. The keys also disable the three monster teleporters in the final level, which skips most of the last battle. Hunt the secret levels; they are the point of the game.

sections.name: Mother Demon
sections.card: The final boss in The Absolution. Her flame trail tosses you into the air where you cannot steer, and four homing rockets follow; taking all four at once kills through any armour. The answer is the fully upgraded Unmaker at point-blank range: its fire rate stuns her so she never launches the rockets, leaving only the flame trails to dodge. Without all three Demon Keys you also fight a large horde before she appears and burn most of your ammo doing it; then it is the BFG on careful timing, or rockets. Get the keys first.

sections.name: The Lost Levels
sections.card: The 2020 re-release's extra episode: six levels that start you stranded with no weapons on a distant base and end in Final Judgement against the Sister Resurrector, plus one separate fun level. It opens when you beat the Mother Demon, or by finishing the secret level Hectic and using the Features menu's level select, or with any password for the first level and the same menu; on PC a -warp 34 launch flag also works. All three Demon Keys and the Unmaker are found again inside Final Judgement and are required to finish it.

sections.name: Starting out in GTA V
sections.card: Three protagonists share one map, and in free roam you can switch between them any time from the character wheel; the number under each face is how many missions that person has waiting, and you cannot switch while you have a wanted level. Each has a special ability on the small yellow meter under the radar: Michael slows time in gunfights, Franklin slows time while driving, Trevor takes half damage and deals double while raging. Skills grow by doing: run to build stamina, land shots to build shooting, punch and play sports for strength. A cheap trick worth knowing early: switch away and straight back, and your character returns with full health and a repaired, cleaned car.

sections.name: Special abilities and how to grow them
sections.card: Michael's Area Kill is bullet time for shootouts and lasts thirty seconds once the ability bar is maxed. Franklin's Driving Focus slows the world while he is in any land vehicle, tank included, and makes gaps and slides easy; it starts at a third of its final length. Trevor's rage doubles his damage and makes him immune to everything for its duration. The bar refills differently for each of them, and the skill behind it grows with use: Franklin's climbs while he drifts, threads near misses at speed, drives into oncoming traffic, or holds ninety percent of a car's top speed. Grow the bar and you grow the time you get.

sections.name: Wanted levels and losing the cops
sections.card: Five stars, not six, and the police are far more persistent than in older games: they ram, box you in, take civilians' cars to keep chasing, and respond to crimes nobody saw because bystanders phone them in. There is no search circle. Every officer has a cone of vision and hunts across the whole map, and the helicopter's cone is enormous, so a chase is lost by breaking every line of sight, not by driving fast in the open. At one star an officer tries to arrest you at gunpoint; fighting or fleeing makes it two on the spot, and security guards and motorcycle cops simply open fire. You cannot switch characters while wanted. If nobody sees you drive into a Los Santos Customs the door opens and the stars go with it; if you were spotted approaching, it stays shut.

sections.name: Skills and the cheapest ways to raise them
sections.card: Seven skills grow by use. Stamina rises one percent every 175 metres run or minute swum, and once it is full you never tire. Shooting rises with hits and headshots, and the Ammu-Nation range gives three percent per gold medal. Strength rises one percent per twenty landed punches, or from golf and tennis. Stealth grows from silent takedowns and creeping. Flying gives one percent per ten minutes in the air, one for each bridge you fly under, and three to five per flight-school gold. Driving rises with air time and clean stunt jumps, two or three percent a jump. Lung capacity gains two percent per minute under water and from yoga. Max out stamina first; the rest follow whatever you already enjoy.

sections.name: Heists: the approach and the crew
sections.card: The big robberies are the spine of the story and the first time the series lets you plan one. Each starts with a choice of approach, quiet from the roof or loud through the front, and a crew you hire rather than recruit: drivers, gunmen and hackers who each want a percentage of the take. Experts cost a bigger slice and perform; cheap newcomers keep more money in your pocket but can fumble the job. Then come setup missions to steal the gear and vehicles the plan needs. Pick the approach that suits how you like to play, and spend on the crew member whose job your plan cannot survive without.

sections.name: Money: the stock market and the assassination jobs
sections.card: The real money in the single-player game is the stock market. Two exchanges exist: the LCN works offline and reacts to what happens in the story, and the BAWSAQ needs a Social Club connection. Five assassination missions for Franklin, unlocked after Fame or Shame, each swing a named company; buy that stock before the hit (or just after, for the bus job), wait while the market ticks every thirty seconds, and sell at the top, often eighty percent up and sometimes far more. Do all but the first of them after the final big score so you are investing a fortune rather than pocket change, then buy the golf club and the cinemas that were out of reach.

sections.name: Properties
sections.card: Buying businesses opens up after Trevor's mission Nervous Ron: walk to the For Sale sign outside and pay. Each pays a weekly sum into its owner's account, and the manager will sometimes phone for help; ignoring the call cuts the week's profit. You need at least five for completion. Early ones that pay back: Franklin's cab company for a steady two thousand a week, and Trevor's McKenzie Field hangar, which pays five to seven thousand per smuggling run. The golf club and cinemas are for after the stock market has made you rich.

sections.name: Side jobs and collectibles that count
sections.card: Not everything on the map matters for completion. Random events (fifty-seven, sixty in the enhanced version) appear as dots: light blue is friendly, red is hostile, flashing lets you choose a side; fourteen count. Strangers and Freaks are the named side stories per character. Of the fifty stunt jumps, twenty-five count; of fifty bridges to fly under, twenty-five, plus eight of the fifteen knife flights. The fifty spaceship parts unlock Omega's mission and the fifty letter scraps solve the Leonora Johnson murder, both optional. Armoured trucks are a quick twenty-five thousand each. The map on the Junk energy drink website lists every jump and fly-under.

sections.name: Weapons, armour and cover
sections.card: You carry every weapon at once, fifty-nine across the base game and updates, and each can take attachments like scopes and suppressors; ammo is kept per weapon class, so an empty pistol does not empty the others. Body armour comes in five tiers from Ammu-Nation, each a fifth stronger than the last, and once you buy a heavier one the lighter ones vanish from the shelf; it does nothing against melee. Cover is one button that snaps you to the nearest solid object; from there you can blind-fire without a reticle, nudge the stick to peek and aim while barely exposed, or slip round a corner without leaving cover.

sections.name: Starting out in GTA IV
sections.card: Liberty City opens up one island at a time as the story goes, starting in Broker. Save by walking to the bed in a safehouse and choosing to sleep; that also clears any wanted level. There are no garages: the yellow Residents Parking bays on the street outside each safehouse hold two vehicles, and anything damaged there repairs itself when you leave the area or reload. Gunfire hurts far more than in older games, so the cover button is not optional: it snaps you to the nearest solid object, and from there you strafe, pop out to aim, or blind-fire round the edge. The phone runs the game: friends call, jobs arrive as texts and emails, and the internet cafés are where the side work starts.

sections.name: Wanted levels and the search circle
sections.card: Six stars. When you are wanted a flashing circle sits on the radar: that is where the police are looking, and every cop inside it is a flashing icon. Get outside the circle without being seen and stay quiet for a few seconds and the stars fade; get spotted leaving and the circle re-centres on you. White stars mean they see you, grey means they have lost you, blinking grey means they are about to give up. Swapping cars buys a couple of seconds at best. While wanted you cannot buy guns or clothes, take a taxi, enter bars or activities, or use the subway above two stars, and getting arrested drops you at the nearest station without your weapons or armour. Pay 'n' Spray clears it if you enter unseen in a car that fits, any bed clears it, and once unlocked a call to Kiki or Francis clears up to three stars.

sections.name: Friends and their favours
sections.card: Each friend has a like rating you raise by taking them out: bowling, darts, pool, eating, drinking, shows, the strip club. You get about an in-game hour to collect them once a date is set, being late costs points, and declining their calls costs five to ten each time. At seventy-five percent they phone to offer a favour. Roman sends a free cab that works even while the police are after you, which is the best escape in the game. Little Jacob drives up with a boot full of guns at sixty percent off, usable mid-mission. Brucie flies you across the city by helicopter. Dwayne, if you let him live, sends two armed men to fight beside you. Packie leaves a car bomb you detonate by phone.

sections.name: Girlfriends
sections.card: Two girlfriends come from the story and three from the dating sites, which open after the mission Out of the Closet: reply to a profile, wait for her email, and the first date decides whether she gives you her number. Each has tastes in clothes, cars and venues that move her fondness, and a bad date or not asking to come in ends it, though she reappears on the site a few days later as if you had never met. The online three pay off: Kiki the lawyer clears wanted levels with a phone call once she is fond of you, Carmen tops up your health by phone, and Alex gets you discounts on clothes. The Algonquin two are unavailable until that island opens.

sections.name: Side jobs: Most Wanted, Stevie's cars and Brucie's exports
sections.card: Sit in a stationary police car and the computer lists ten most-wanted criminals for the region: thirty in all across Algonquin, the Broker-Dukes-Bohan side, and Alderney, in any order you like. Stevie texts thirty car requests with a photo of where each is parked, usually within a block of the hint; deliver them undamaged to his lot in Bohan for the best money, nearly four hundred thousand in total, once you have the Alderney safehouse and have done Smackdown and No. 1. Brucie emails ten exotic cars to steal for his lockup in East Hook, a thousand each, eight hundred for bikes, less if you dent them. The Fixer's payphone in Port Tudor, Alderney, hands out assassinations after Truck Hustle. None of these are the story; all of them are the hundred percent.

sections.name: Collectibles: flying rats and stunt jumps
sections.card: Two hundred pigeons are hidden around Liberty City and Alderney, glowing red and cooing so you can find them at night; shoot, burn, blow up or run over every one and the Annihilator attack helicopter spawns on the MeTV building. There are also fifty stunt jumps, and unlike the pigeons all fifty are needed for completion. The game tells you after each landing: Stunt jump completed, or Not good enough. Some only need you to land; others want a distance or a precise landing spot that the game never explains, so a jump that keeps failing usually wants more speed or a different line rather than more attempts.

sections.name: Weapons and where to buy them
sections.card: Sixteen weapons in two tiers each, with generic names: the carbine is the M4, the assault rifle the AK. Dropped guns lie on the ground with a faint orange glow, and you can disarm an enemy by shooting his hand rather than killing him. The underground gun shops open after Do You Have Protection?, and once Little Jacob likes you enough his van sells everything at sixty percent off. Fixed spawn points around the city refill the same weapon every visit, which is how most players keep an RPG. Body armour is sold alongside the guns and is the difference between two hits and five.

sections.name: Liberty City's boroughs and when they open
sections.card: Four boroughs of the real New York plus New Jersey, each with a different feel: Broker is Brooklyn and where you start, Dukes is Queens on the same island, Bohan is the Bronx across the water, Algonquin is Manhattan with the tall buildings and most of the money, and the State of Alderney is New Jersey, industrial and suburban. The bridges are closed by the police at first: Algonquin opens after the mission Blow Your Cover and Alderney after Three Leaf Clover. Crossing a closed bridge earns an instant six-star wanted level, so if the map shows a closed island, the story has to get there first.

sections.name: Starting out in Fallout: New Vegas
sections.card: Doc Mitchell patches you up in Goodsprings, sets your stats with his tester, and hands over a Pip-Boy and a gun or two based on the skills you tagged. The town is the tutorial: Sunny Smiles teaches shooting and campfire cooking, and the little quests around it show every kind of skill check in the game, all of them fixed thresholds rather than dice rolls, so a Speech of 25 either works or it does not. The road north out of town is closed by deathclaws at the quarry past Sloan; the game means you to go south through Primm, Nipton and Novac and round the long way. Doc Mitchell's containers are safe storage, and once the town is cleared nothing hostile respawns inside it. You choose three tag skills for fifteen points each, get ten skill points plus half your Intelligence per level, a perk every two levels, and a cap of thirty, or fifty with the four add-ons.

sections.name: Hardcore mode
sections.card: Switch it on from the options at any time, and off again the same way; finishing the game with it on earns the achievement. Stimpaks and RadAway heal over time instead of instantly, a doctor's bag only partly mends a crippled limb, and otherwise only a doctor, certain beds, a healing poultice or Hydra will, so sleeping in an owned bed for the Well Rested bonus becomes the free fix. Ammunition has weight. Companions can die for good. You also drink, eat and sleep: thirst climbs fastest, about one point every ten real seconds, and each stage strips stats until the top one kills you. Fast travel is allowed but the hours it takes still count, so check your meters before a long jump or you can arrive dead. Campfire food heals far more than stimpaks once your Survival is decent, which is the whole point of the skill.

sections.name: Reputation, disguises and hit squads
sections.card: Every town and faction keeps two separate tallies, fame and infamy, and your title with them (Accepted, Liked, Idolized, or Shunned, Vilified, or a mixed one) comes from the pair. Being caught stealing costs two infamy; killing one of theirs in the open costs thirty. Killing from hiding with a silent one-shot kill, or with the Mister Sandman perk, costs nothing, except with the Brotherhood, who notice everything but Sandman. Wearing a faction's armour turns your standing with them neutral while it is on, a disguise that also hides some other relationships from your Pip-Boy. Fall to Shunned with the Legion and squads of four assassins start walking across the map to find you; anger the NCR too and Ranger squads join them. Infamy with the NCR and Legion can each be wiped once, when their leaders invite you in after the events at the Tops.

sections.name: Deathclaws and Quarry Junction
sections.card: The quarry past Sloan is why the road north is closed. Inside are ordinary deathclaws at double or triple their usual health, young ones, an alpha male whose swipe does three hundred damage, and a mother with a litter of babies who goes berserk if you kill one in front of her. Both entrances are guarded. They stop chasing if you stand on a rock they cannot reach or dive into water, a crippled leg stops the leaping attack and slows them to a limp, and a flare gun makes them flee. The reward for clearing it is a Fat Man with two mini nukes and a light machine gun in the den. Come back much later, with the anti-materiel rifle the Gun Runners' guard brags about, and remember Dead Wind Cavern holds the legendary one, which hits twice as hard.

sections.name: Cazadores
sections.card: Giant orange wasps in swarms of four or more, flying fast and erratic, and their sting does more raw damage than a giant radscorpion's and three times the poison, for longer. You will not sneak past them: their perception is higher than a deathclaw's. Cripple a wing in V.A.T.S. and one drops out of the air and slows to a crawl; crippling the antennae only frenzies them, and headshots give no bonus. Carry antivenom or super stimpaks, and know that your companions cannot use antivenom, so heal them with stimpaks from the companion wheel; they will use datura antivenom if they have it. The ones inside the Big MT are tougher still.

sections.name: Night stalkers
sections.card: Coyote bodies with rattlesnake heads, made in a lab and now everywhere at night and in caves, especially their dens, where the packs are large and the tunnels twist. They leap and bite with venom weaker than a cazador's, but it stacks if several land, so treat the poison. They rattle and hiss when close, which is your warning, and their standing bite animation roots them for a moment, so backpedal out of it. With the Animal Friend perk they ignore you entirely. The pack in Charleston Cave can turn invisible like a Stealth Boy; fight those in a corridor where they have to come to you.

sections.name: Companions and what each one gives you
sections.card: You can bring one person and one of the two non-humans at once, ordered through the companion wheel, and none of them care about your karma except Cass, who leaves if you go properly evil. In normal mode they only fall unconscious. Boone, the sniper in the dinosaur at Novac, gives Spotter, which lights up hostiles while you aim. ED-E, the broken eyebot in the Nash house at Primm, extends how far you detect enemies. Veronica at the 188 Trading Post lets you use a workbench anywhere. Rex, the cyberdog with the Kings in Freeside, marks nearby loot. Cass at the Mojave Outpost makes whiskey harmless and armouring. Raul, locked up on Black Mountain, slows your gear's wear. Lily at Jacobstown makes Stealth Boys last and sneak crits hurt. Arcade at the Old Mormon Fort makes stimpaks heal more.

sections.name: Getting into the Strip
sections.card: The north gate is held by Securitrons who shoot anyone who walks up without talking to the greeter. Ways in: pass the credit check by carrying two thousand caps, which are checked, not taken; hack the greeter with a Science of eighty; hand over a passport, forged by Ralph at Mick and Ralph's in Freeside for five hundred caps, three hundred and seventy-five with a Barter of fifty, or free with a good NCR reputation, or free from the King as his favour after G.I. Blues; or shoot every robot at the gate, which earns Strip infamy for each one and turns every Securitron inside hostile. Once through, Victor finds you at the door, and the Tops, Gomorrah, the Ultra-Luxe, Vault 21 and the NCR Embassy are all a short walk.

sections.name: Weapon mods and the unique guns you can get early
sections.card: Mods never turn up as loot: you buy them from a dozen stationary and travelling merchants whose stock rotates every three days, and each weapon takes up to three, one of each kind, fixed forever once attached. Unique weapons refuse mods but come with better stats and sometimes the mods built in. Early ones worth a detour: Lucky, a .357 that never jams, in a hard-locked floor safe behind the gift shop counter of the Bison Steve in Primm; That Gun, bought or stolen from the Dino Bite gift shop in Novac; Ratslayer, a silenced night-scoped varmint rifle with a huge critical multiplier, in the Broc Flower Cave past the giant rats; This Machine, the Garand, for the quiet quest about Sergeant Contreras at Camp McCarran. Uniques cannot be repaired with their common cousins unless you take Jury Rigging at Repair ninety, which repairs anything with anything of the same class.

sections.name: Skills, SPECIAL points, implants and books
sections.card: Each skill starts at two plus twice its governing stat plus half your Luck, so Luck quietly lifts everything. Three tagged skills get fifteen points; each level gives ten plus half your Intelligence; and the base game does not hand out enough to max them all, so choose. Skill books are three permanent points each, four with Comprehension, and there are about fifty-two of them; magazines are ten points for a minute, doubled and tripled by the matching perks, and merchants sell them, so carry a few for a hard check. Doctor Usanagi at the New Vegas medical clinic near the Crimson Caravan sells a permanent point in any stat for four thousand caps each, as many as your Endurance allows, plus armour under the skin for eight thousand and slow health regeneration for twelve. Buy the Intelligence implant first if you can afford it; it pays itself back in skill points.

sections.name: Snow globes and star bottle caps
sections.card: Seven snow globes are hidden in the base game and each is worth two thousand caps from Jane at the Lucky 38, where they go on a display stand; finding all seven is the achievement, selling them is optional. They sit on the rubble-topped grave in Goodsprings cemetery, the welcome desk of the Hoover Dam visitor centre, upstairs in the tower of the Old Mormon Fort, the reception desk of the Jacobstown lodge, the table inside the Boomers' museum at Nellis, the counter of the Lucky 38 cocktail lounge, and one more at the test site. The blue-star Sunset Sarsaparilla caps are a different hunt: one bottle in twenty holds one, over a hundred sit in fixed spots, and fifty of them buy the legendary prize at the company headquarters, though collectors, as Malcolm Holmes warns you, will kill for them.

sections.name: Starting out in Super Mario 64
sections.card: The paintings in the castle are the courses: walk up and the surface ripples, jump in and you are there. Each course holds several missions, one star each, and stars open the castle's doors. Health is the eight-wedge power meter, refilled by coins, spinning hearts, or surfacing in water. The moves are the game: run and jump three times for the triple jump, run then crouch and jump for the long jump, jump into a wall and jump again for the wall kick, crouch and jump for the backflip, turn around sharply and jump for the side flip, and press crouch in the air to ground-pound. Caps last sixty seconds and only appear in courses once you have hit their switches. A hundred coins in any course is an extra star, and the rabbit in the basement gives one when caught at fifteen stars and again at fifty.

sections.name: Bowser: the three fights
sections.card: The first fight opens at eight stars. Bowser breathes a stream of fire that leaves burning sparks, jumps to shake the ground, which stuns you unless you are in the air, and claws if you stand close. Get behind him, grab his tail, spin the stick to build speed, and throw him into one of the four spiked bombs around the edge; a miss and he climbs back on. The second fight, after boarding the sub, adds a stage that tilts whenever he lands, single fireballs, and teleporting. The final fight at seventy stars has five bombs, and he must be thrown three times: his slams now send shockwaves along the floor, and he breathes fire upward that rains back down. The keys from the first two fights open the locked doors.

sections.name: King Bob-omb and the Whomp King
sections.card: King Bob-omb waits on the summit of Bob-omb Battlefield. He grabs and throws you if you walk into his hands, so circle behind him, pick him up and throw him; three throws win. Throw him off the mountain and he calls it cheating and the fight restarts, and he can hurt you on contact in the moment he gets up. The Whomp King on top of Whomp's Fortress attacks by falling flat on his face, which is your opening: ground-pound his back while he is down, three times, and the star is yours and a tower rises on the fortress.

sections.name: Eyerok, the Big Bully and the Wiggler
sections.card: Eyerok is the pair of stone hands in the pyramid at Shifting Sand Land. Each hand slams or shoves on its own and only one opens its eye at a time; punch, kick or dive into the open eye, three hits destroys that hand, and both must go for the star. A hit from him costs three wedges. The Big Bully in Lethal Lava Land cannot hurt you and you cannot hurt him: he shoves, and you win by punching him off the platform into the lava. The Wiggler lives inside Tiny-Huge Island's mountain: ground-pound the pool on the tiny side to flood his house, then go in on the huge side and jump on his head.

sections.name: The three caps
sections.card: Each cap needs its switch pressed in a hidden course before its blocks turn solid anywhere else. The red Wing Cap, from the tower at ten stars, lets you fly from a triple jump or a cannon shot, slowly losing height. The green Metal Cap makes you invulnerable and very heavy: you sink and walk along the bottom, never need to breathe, and cannot swim. The blue Vanish Cap makes you a ghost for a short time, walking through enemies and metal fences. All caps run out after a minute, and finishing a mission drops the form. Dire, Dire Docks is the one place you can wear metal and vanish at once.

sections.name: Stars that are easy to miss
sections.card: Catch the yellow rabbit in the castle basement when you have fifteen stars, and again at fifty, and he hands over a star each time; he never comes back after the second. Every course also has a star for collecting a hundred coins in one visit, which is where most of the total comes from. The wing-cap tower's own star is its eight red coins, in pairs at the compass points, and you will have to land and relaunch because you lose height as you fly. Tick Tock Clock runs at whatever speed the clock hands showed when you jumped in, so choose your moment at the painting to freeze or slow the machinery.

sections.name: Starting out in Mario Kart 64
sections.card: Hold the gas as the lights change from red to blue for a rocket start; too early and you spin your tyres and leave slower than everyone. Hop and hold to drift, then wiggle the stick side to side while sliding: the smoke goes white, yellow, then orange, and letting go on orange gives a mini-turbo. Gas and brake together spins the kart on the spot. If you drive straight into a banana, a well-timed tap of the brake saves the spin and shows a musical note. Item boxes hand out stronger items the further back you are. Grand Prix is four cups of four races at 50, 100 and 150cc, scoring nine, six, three and one point for the top four; the Extra class runs the courses mirrored. Battle mode gives each player three balloons, and time-trial ghosts only save if you never pause, crash, reverse or fall.

sections.name: Items and who gets them
sections.card: Your place decides your items. The blue Spiny Shell only comes to fourth place or lower: it runs along the ground with a siren, homes on the leader, flips anyone in its path, and can be held behind your kart to block other shells before you fire it. Lightning goes to second through eighth: everyone else shrinks, cannot use mushrooms, stars or Boos, and can be flattened if you drive over them. Fake Item Boxes belong to first and second: an upside-down question mark, they launch whoever hits them and block incoming shells. Triple red shells orbit you, fire one at a time, and shield you meanwhile. Bananas dropped in a trail take out the whole line if a kart clips the first.

sections.name: Shortcuts worth learning
sections.card: On Rainbow Road, hop over the left railing right at the start to land on the loop around the big star and skip a huge stretch. On Royal Raceway the dash ramp before the second row of item boxes cuts a corner; a mushroom does it, or a left drift with a full mini-turbo released into a hop. In Yoshi Valley, hop left where the routes rejoin to skip a bend, and use a mushroom across the last off-road patch, drifting into the fence for a bigger boost onto the final straight. In Kalimari Desert you can follow the train tracks into the tunnel and turn around with a star to skip most of a lap, but never on the final lap. Nearly every corner on Royal Raceway has a dirt patch a mushroom crosses.

sections.name: Courses that fight back
sections.card: Toad's Turnpike is the third longest track and a figure of eight full of traffic: cars, tankers, box trucks and school buses that never stop. Kalimari Desert crosses the railway twice, so listen for the train. Choco Mountain drops boulders on the left U-turn. Yoshi Valley splits into six routes; the leftmost is the simplest but has no railings. Frappe Snowland has a river jump on the straight and a field of snowmen that stop a kart dead. Rainbow Road is long, unwalled in places, and the Chain Chomps on it are the reason to learn the start shortcut.

sections.name: Starting out in Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door
sections.card: Battles are turn-based on a theatre stage: Mario and one partner each act every turn, and you can swap who goes first, which also puts that one in front. Hit an enemy in the field to open with a free first strike; they can do the same to you. Every attack has an action command, a button press at the right moment for extra damage, and every enemy attack can be guarded with A as it lands for one less damage, or superguarded with B in a tiny window for no damage and a point back. Levelling up every hundred star points gives a choice: five HP, five FP or three badge points. The boots and hammer upgrades are story finds you cannot skip, and the black chests hand out paper tricks like the plane and the sideways squeeze.

sections.name: Star Power, Stylish moves and the crowd
sections.card: The audience is a resource. Every jump, hammer and partner attack earns Star Power for the Crystal Star moves, and it comes faster when you land the action command or add a Stylish move, an extra press at the right beat of the attack animation that makes the crowd cheer; Stylish works only on normal and badge attacks, not items or counters. Appeal to gain Star Power directly while anyone is awake in the seats. Your star rank sets how many can attend, rising at levels ten, twenty and thirty. The crowd is not always friendly: some throw things at you or heckle, and Hooktail, Cortez and the Shadow Queen eat audience members to heal, so clear them first.

sections.name: Badges and BP
sections.card: Badges are the build. You find them in red question blocks, take them from enemies, buy them at the Lovely Howz in Rogueport, from Charlieton at steep prices, at the Pianta Parlor for tokens, or from Dazzle underground for Star Pieces. Each costs badge points to wear, so BP at level-up is often the best pick. P badges give the same effect to your partner. Wearing two copies of an attack badge doubles its FP cost but raises its power. The ones people build around: Power Bounce, repeated jumps until you miss a command; Multibounce, one hit on every enemy; Quake Hammer for everything on the ground; and Power Rush, Close Call and Last Stand, which only work while you are in Danger at five HP or less, plus Mega Rush at exactly one, which is why some players have Chet Rippo lower their maximum HP on purpose.

sections.name: Hooktail
sections.card: The dragon at the top of the castle in chapter one, guarding the first Crystal Star: twenty HP, one point of defence, five attack, and a trick where she plays dead and comes back with ten more. She eats members of the audience to heal, so keep the crowd thin, and her bite cannot be blocked at all, so keep your own HP topped up rather than hoping to guard. Somewhere in her castle is a badge that changes your attack sound to a cricket's chirp, and the thief who mentions it is right: the noise makes her flinch. Koops joins you for this fight; his shell toss hits her first before you commit Mario. Fire hurts her badly.

sections.name: Rawk Hawk, Magnus von Grapple and Cortez
sections.card: Rawk Hawk, the Glitz Pit champion in chapter three, fights from the air: a flipping jump, a flying elbow, a slide kick on the ground, and a ceiling hang that shakes down a rain of objects for one damage each, which Koops's shell ignores. Magnus von Grapple, the robot at the end of chapter two, stomps one party member for two base damage every turn until it drops to twenty HP, then fires its fists off as separate targets. Cortez, the pirate skeleton under Keelhaul Key in chapter five, comes in three forms, and beating him settles nothing because he is already dead; the fight ends when he understands you only want the Crystal Star, not his treasure.

sections.name: Rogueport's side content: Shine Sprites, the Pit and the Trouble Center
sections.card: Forty-two Shine Sprites are hidden in blocks across the world, and Merlon next to Professor Frankly trades three of them for a partner rank; each of the seven partners can go up twice, and Merluvlee the fortune teller will point you at the ones you missed. The Trouble Center on the east side of town is a bulletin board of odd jobs that pay coins, items and badges. Under the town lies the Pit of a Hundred Trials: a hundred floors of fights with Charlieton selling supplies part-way down and Bonetail at the bottom, whose breaths freeze, confuse, shrink or sleep you unless you guard them or raise Shell Shield; she coughs up the Return Postage badge. Zess T. in the square cooks any two ingredients into something better.

sections.name: Starting out in Pikmin 2
sections.card: There is no day limit this time: the goal is ten thousand Pokos of treasure to clear the company's debt, and treasures and enemy bodies both pay. Two captains share the work, and the button that used to pause now swaps between them, so one can carry while the other fights. The day still ends at sunset, and any Pikmin not with a captain or back at the Onion is eaten when the night creatures wake, so watch the sun and call everyone in early. The colours: red for fire and the hardest hitters, yellow thrown highest and safe from electricity, blue the only ones for water, purple heavy and strong, white fast, poison-proof and able to see treasure buried underground. Bulbmin, found only in certain caves, shrug off every hazard but cannot leave with you.

sections.name: Caves
sections.card: Most of the treasure is underground. A cave is a stack of small floors, each laid out fresh from random pieces every time you enter, with a hole down at the end and usually a boss on the last floor and a geyser home afterwards. There is no Onion below, so the squad you walk in with is the squad you have; nothing you collect counts until you come back up, and leaving early forfeits the run. The day's clock stops while you are down there, which makes a cave the right place to spend a late afternoon. Read the hazard icons at the entrance and bring the colours that match, and bring purples for the fights.

sections.name: Purple and White Pikmin
sections.card: Purples weigh as much as ten Pikmin, so one lifts what ten would, and some treasures, including the map pieces that open new areas at over a hundred weight, are impossible without them. Their landing on an enemy stuns it, they hit hard, and blowhog gusts do not move them, but they are slow and fly low when thrown. Whites are the fastest Pikmin, immune to poison and able to dig up treasure that is completely buried, which no other colour can find; anything that eats one is poisoned. Both come only from candypop buds in caves, in limited numbers, so treat them as tools rather than an army and keep them out of the front line.

sections.name: Sprays and nectar
sections.card: The purple ultra-bitter spray, ten purple berries from a Burgeoning Spiderwort or a found dose, turns every enemy near you to stone for about nine seconds, bomb rocks included, and is the answer to anything you cannot outfight; the purple-berry plants are rarer than the red ones, so hoard it. The red ultra-spicy spray, ten red berries, sends your Pikmin into a frenzy, faster and stronger, and flowers them. Nectar does the flowering on its own: drops from eggs, rubble, nectar weed and some insects, and a flowered Pikmin runs and carries noticeably faster than a leaf, so let a new batch drink before a long carry.

sections.name: Empress Bulblax and the Snagrets
sections.card: The Empress Bulblax is a bulborb the size of the room. In the Hole of Heroes she is asleep when you arrive, which is your sneak attack; in Frontier Cavern she is awake and pumping out larvae without end, so kill the mother, not the children. She rolls from wall to wall, so keep the squad off the sides and throw purples at her head in the pauses. The Burrowing Snagret hides under the ground until you are close, then rises to peck; it often gets stuck half out, and a stuck snagret is free damage, again best done with purples. Its big cousin the Pileated Snagret pulls fully out and walks after you.

sections.name: Beady Long Legs, Man-at-Legs and Raging Long Legs
sections.card: The arachnorbs are all legs and one body, and only the body counts. The Beady Long Legs falls from the sky when you enter its ground and stomps about, crushing anything under a foot; it stops to lower its body to rest, and that is when you throw yellows high onto it, then whistle them back before it shakes. The Man-at-Legs is different: half-buried, it only wakes when touched, it never crushes, and instead a gun unfolds that tracks the captain you are controlling, so keep the squad in cover behind the pillars, swap captains to draw fire, and attack the body when it settles. The Raging Long Legs in the Hole of Heroes has huge feet but leaves room underneath its belly if you stay close.

sections.name: The Waterwraith and the Submerged Castle
sections.card: The castle's mouth is under water, so only blues may enter, and inside are all four hazards; take about sixty blues if you also want the Bulbmin living there. On each of the first four floors, five minutes after you arrive, the Waterwraith drops in on its stone rollers and hunts you, crushing Pikmin and other creatures alike, and nothing hurts it but purples or a petrifying spray. So each floor is a race: find the hole down before the clock, and grab treasure only if it is on the way. On the last floor it appears when you enter its arena, and there you fight it, purples first to knock it off its rollers.

sections.name: Titan Dweevil
sections.card: The final boss, at the bottom of the Dream Den, carries four weapons that are the four hazards: a flame cannon, an electric shocker, a water pump and a poison bomb, and each becomes a treasure when it falls. It is tall, so throw yellows to reach the weapons, and pull them back the moment a weapon starts up; captains sidestep the hazards. Do not let Pikmin swarm its feet, they go idle there and die. Once the weapons are gone the body is open. It stops to rest after two or three rounds of stomping, and it only reacts to attacks once a stomping cycle has finished.

sections.name: Segmented Crawbster
sections.card: The boss of the Cavern of Chaos, on floor ten. It drops from above when something walks under it, then rolls itself into a ball and charges the captain you are controlling, not the Pikmin, homing all the way. You cannot hurt it while it rolls; you make it hurt itself: stand with a wall behind you and step aside at the last moment so it slams in, then attack the soft belly while it is flipped. Boulders fall as the fight goes on and sometimes eggs with them. Swap captains to pull its charge where you want it.

sections.name: The enemies that empty a squad
sections.card: Spotty Bulbears never sleep in this game: they patrol with dwarf bulbears trailing behind, and they heal if you leave them, so it is all or nothing, and purples from the side. Gatling Groinks fire mortars from range, some from towers you cannot reach, and a dead one left lying gets back up. The Careening Dirigibug floats over and drops a bomb rock at your feet; kill it in the two seconds it takes to produce one or step back. Anode Beetles are harmless alone and lethal in pairs, when an arc jumps between them that only yellows survive. Volatile Dweevils drop from the ceiling near treasure and explode after a short chase. The Bumbling Snitchbug picks up a captain and scatters the squad, so keep moving under it.

sections.name: Starting out in Melee
sections.card: Twenty-five fighters, fourteen there from the start and eleven to unlock, on twenty-nine stages. You do not drain a health bar: damage climbs as a percentage, and the higher it goes the further a hit sends you, so a stock is lost by being launched past the edge of the screen, not by running out of health. Everything is faster than the first game: less freeze on hits, higher gravity, faster falls, and momentum carried out of a dash into a jump. Smash attacks charge for up to a second for forty percent more power. Shield with the shoulder buttons, and press them only part way for a bigger, longer-lasting but weaker shield. Sudden Death after a tie restarts at three hundred percent, where nearly anything is a knockout.

sections.name: The techniques the game never tells you about
sections.card: Melee's depth is in inputs it never mentions. L-cancelling: press a shoulder button or Z within seven frames of landing during an air attack and the landing animation plays twice as fast, halving your lag. Wavedashing: air-dodge diagonally into the ground and you slide a short way while able to do any grounded action, which is how spacing and shield pressure work at a high level; Luigi slides furthest, then the Ice Climbers and Mewtwo. Dash dancing flicks back and forth to bait a commitment. Short hop, done by releasing jump during the crouch before it, keeps aerials low and fast. Fast falling, a tap down while falling, ends a jump early and beats an opponent's timing.

sections.name: Surviving hits: DI, SDI and teching
sections.card: You are not helpless when hit. Hold the stick during the freeze frames before you are launched and you shift your angle by up to about eighteen degrees; hold perpendicular to the knockback to live longer, or along it to fall out of a combo. Tap the stick during the freeze itself and you slide a small distance each tap, which is how you escape multi-hit moves; this is a separate trick from the first. When you are about to hit the ground, a wall, or a ceiling while tumbling, press a shoulder button within twenty frames to tech: you bounce up briefly untouchable instead of lying there, and a tech left or right rolls you away. Teching a wall while falling off the side is how you survive being spiked, and holding jump as you do it wall-jumps you back.

sections.name: Edgeguarding and the ledge
sections.card: Most stocks are taken off the stage, not on it. When someone is knocked off, you go out or wait for them: hit them again, or take the ledge yourself so they cannot grab it, which forces them onto the stage where you are waiting. Grabbing the ledge gives you invincible frames, and the ledge dash, dropping off then jumping and air-dodging back on at the right moment, keeps some of those frames while skipping the slow climb animation. Meteor smashes hit straight down and are the cleanest kills off stage; you can cancel one by jumping or using your up special eight frames after the hit stops, which is your escape when it happens to you.

sections.name: Shields, grabs and punishing
sections.card: Blocking is not passive. Shields stop everything but grabs and a few unblockable moves, and a light press makes a bigger shield that resists being poked through but leaves you worse off afterwards. The standard punish is the shield grab, pressing attack while shielding, which skips the delay of dropping the shield and catches an opponent stuck in the end of their move. Out of shield you can also jump, roll, wavedash, up smash or use an aerial, and how good those are decides how safe an attack is against you. Grabs lead into throws, and a few characters chain them: Sheik's down throw regrabs most of the cast from zero, and the Ice Climbers can hold you in place indefinitely with the wobble, which many tournaments ban.

sections.name: Fox and Falco
sections.card: The two Star Fox characters sit at the top of the game. Fox is the fastest lightweight in it: second fastest dash, third fastest fall, three-frame jump, and a shield reflector that comes out instantly and knocks people sideways off the stage. His speed is also his weakness, since falling fast means being combo'd hard. Falco is his slower, heavier twin with a different feel: his laser makes people flinch and cancels when he lands, which shuts down approaches, and his down air spikes straight down. The Falco pillar, reflector into a down air spike into more, is one of the best shield-wearing routines in the game. Both die early because they fall so fast.

sections.name: Marth, Sheik, Jigglypuff and Peach
sections.card: Marth kills with the tip of his sword and nothing else; spacing is the whole character, and the Ken combo, a forward air then a jump and a down air spike, is the classic finish and needs the first hit placed exactly. Sheik is fast, combos easily, and chain-throws much of the cast from zero, though only a few of her moves actually kill. Jigglypuff is slow on the ground and floats in the air; the wall of pain, back air after back air while drifting out with them, carries people off the stage, and Rest hits on the first frame for twenty-eight percent and kills under fifteen, but leaves it asleep and helpless if it misses. Peach fights almost entirely in the air, with a float, a down smash that shreds, and turnips she pulls from the ground.

sections.name: Unlocking the other eleven
sections.card: Every hidden character has to be beaten in a fight before joining, and each has two ways to summon that fight. Jigglypuff, Dr. Mario, Falco, Young Link, Pichu, Luigi, Ganondorf, Mewtwo, Roy, Marth and Mr. Game and Watch are the eleven. Some come from playing modes: Jigglypuff after any single-player mode, Marth after using all fourteen starters in any mode, Dr. Mario after Classic as Mario with no continues, Roy the same as Marth, Young Link after ten characters have cleared a mode, Falco after the hundred-man melee. Others come from events: Ganondorf from event twenty-nine, Pichu from event thirty-seven. Luigi wants the first Adventure stage finished with a two as the second digit of the seconds. Mewtwo wants twenty hours of versus play, less with more players, and Mr. Game and Watch wants every other character to clear a mode.

sections.name: The single-player modes and what they unlock
sections.card: Classic is eleven fights ending with Master Hand, who has a health bar rather than a percentage; take half of it inside five minutes and fifty seconds on Normal or higher and Crazy Hand joins him. Adventure is the longer one, with side-scrolling stages between the fights, and if you reach Bowser on Normal or higher within eighteen minutes he comes back as Giga Bowser, worth a hundred thousand points and his own trophy if you beat him without continuing. All-Star opens once every fighter is unlocked and sends you through all of them with a small supply of healing between rounds. Clearing it unlocks Battlefield; clearing all fifty-one event matches unlocks Final Destination. Those two flat stages are what tournaments play on.

sections.name: The opening tram ride and where it leads
sections.card: Black Mesa opens with a long tram ride that needs no input beyond looking around; it carries you from the surface entrance through checkpoints and cargo bays into the underground facility, and doubles as an unskippable loading screen for the level ahead. Step off at the platform, badge through the checkpoint, and follow the corridor signs to the locker room, where you change into the orange HEV suit before the day's work — the path there is linear, so a door that will not open yet is one you have not reached the switch for. Anomalous Materials, the lab down the following hall, is where the real gameplay opens up: once things go wrong there, the crowbar on the floor nearby is the first weapon in the game, and from then on every locked vent or wooden crate is worth swinging at before hunting for another way around.

sections.name: Recharging the HEV suit
sections.card: The suit's own charge, shown on the HUD next to health, does not come back on its own; you top it up at a wall-mounted suit charger, an orange unit with a black charging cord and the HEV logo, kept separate from the white health chargers with the red cross. Walk up and hold use; a mechanical arm extends and feeds power in until you back away or the charger runs dry. Each charger holds a limited reserve that does not refill once spent, so treat the first one in an area as insurance for what is ahead rather than something to top off out of habit, and look for a charger before a big fight rather than after taking damage in it. When a charger's screen goes dark, it is done for good.

sections.name: Crossing the electrified waste pools
sections.card: The waste-treatment area has stretches of standing water with live wiring dropped into it, and the current is constant — there is no safe moment and no warning cycle to wait for. Stepping in deals continuous shock damage until you get out or die, so treat the flooded floor like lava rather than something to time. Cross on anything above the water: desks, cabinets, shelves, floating crates and overhead pipes all work, and the route is usually built into the room once you look up. Better still, cut the power — a red wall switch, breaker or lever, usually just outside the flooded area or at its far end, makes the water safe for good. Where a gap is too wide to jump, push or carry loose wooden crates into the water and use them as stepping stones.

sections.name: Leaving the Forgotten Crossroads
sections.card: The tutorial descent leaves you in the Forgotten Crossroads, the caved-in area right under Dirtmouth, and the easy next step is west: breaking through toward Greenpath opens the first of Hallownest's main regions and gives you the early platforming and enemies that put the Mothwing Cloak dash to use once you pick it up there. The Crossroads also connect east to Crystal Peak's lower entrance and south toward the Fungal Wastes and a tram line to the City of Tears, but those areas expect more health and a spare charm slot or two, so treat them as later stops rather than the first move. Nothing here is one-way for long: a bench near each entrance lets you rest, and fast travel opens up once a stag station nearby is found, so exploring a dead end costs time rather than progress.

sections.name: Choosing a vehicle upgrade at Los Santos Customs
sections.card: Los Santos Customs sells five performance categories per vehicle: engine, brakes, transmission, turbo and armour, plus cosmetic changes that do not affect handling. For a car you actually drive around rather than race, armour and brakes are the upgrades that pay off first: armour buys a few more hits before an explosion totals the car, and better brakes matter more than raw top speed on the city's tight corners. Turbo is worth adding once the engine is already maxed, since it sharpens acceleration out of every corner rather than raising top speed alone; engine level four is the expensive one and the biggest single jump in speed, so it is the upgrade to save for rather than buy first if funds are short. Whichever you pick, storing the car in an owned garage is what keeps the upgrades between sessions.

sections.name: Getting into Fort Zancudo without a wanted level
sections.card: The military base sits under its own airspace rule: fly a plane or helicopter over it at high altitude and ground control has nothing to warn you about, so no wanted level. Drop low or hover and one of the two ground checkpoints radios a warning before opening fire, and going in by road or over the perimeter fence gets you spotted within moments once you are inside, pulling every soldier and vehicle on site down on you at once, wanted level and all. If you only need eyes on what is inside — the jets, the vehicles, the layout — a high pass over the runway is the safe way to look without waking anyone up; landing or setting foot on the ground is what turns it into a fight.

sections.name: Foot chases through construction sites
sections.card: Niko's sprint has a stamina meter that drains fast and recovers slowly, so trying to win a chase by simply outrunning the target on a flat street usually fails. The better approach is cutting distance on stairs, ramps and scaffolding, where the target has to slow down for the same jumps and ladders you do. GTA IV's physics treat most ledges and rails as something to vault or climb rather than clip through, so tap the action button at a waist-high obstacle to hop it instead of running into it, and take stairs over a ladder when you can, since ladders are slower to mount. A fleeing target on foot tends to cut toward the nearest vehicle or a way down to street level, so cutting off the exits rather than chasing in a straight line closes the gap faster. If the mission lets you draw a weapon, a couple of shots to slow the target down beats catching up on foot entirely.

sections.name: Getting across Liberty City fast
sections.card: Once taxi rides unlock after Bull in a China Shop, hailing one from the street lets you skip the drive entirely: pick a destination on the in-car terminal and choose the trip-skip option, and the game cuts straight to arriving, at double the fare. The same terminal has a "hurry" option if you would rather watch the drive and get there sooner, with the driver ignoring traffic laws along the way. If you would rather not wait for a cab to show up at all, the subway threads most of the map and boarding one at a station is quick and cheap, though it only stops where the lines run. Once Niko's friendship with Roman passes 60% after that same mission, calling him for a car service sends a free cab to your marker instead of needing to hail one on the street.

sections.name: Choosing early armor by Damage Threshold, not by looks
sections.card: New Vegas grades armor by Damage Threshold (DT), a flat amount subtracted from every hit, rather than the percentage-based system other Fallout games use, so a lighter suit with real DT can outlast a bulkier one that has none. Leather armor is the standout early pick: DT 6, only fifteen pounds, and on sale from Chet at the Goodsprings general store before you have even left the tutorial area, which already blunts most hits from raiders, geckos and gunslingers to a fraction of their listed damage. Check an item's DT and weight in the Pip-Boy rather than judging by how heavy or armoured it looks — several early "upgrades" carry less DT than leather for a lot more weight. Faction armors like NCR trooper or Great Khan gear are worth grabbing once you can get them, but they are a later upgrade, not a reason to skip leather now.

sections.name: Crossing the crater radiation pools
sections.card: Nine of the atomic warheads fired at Las Vegas during the war missed their target and left radioactive craters scattered across the Mojave, and the pools of water sitting at the bottom of them are the dangerous part: readings up to twenty rads a second in places, high enough to rack up crippling radiation sickness in well under a minute. Check the Geiger counter on the Pip-Boy before committing to a route through one — the rocky rim usually has a dry path around, even if it means climbing rather than walking straight across. RadAway and Rad-X handle the exposure if you do end up wading through, but Rad-X only helps if you take it before you are in the water, not after. The loot at the bottom of a few of these craters is rarely worth crossing for without one of those first.

sections.name: The final battle: hands, patterns and the charge tell
sections.card: The two hands in the final fight are separate targets with only five HP and seven attack each, so killing one is easy, but it comes back on the following turn — treat them as removable nuisances between the main attacks rather than as kills that stick. Watch for the move that raises attack and defence by three, and for the flash that warns of a bigger charged strike a turn ahead of it landing: guard or superguard the turn it actually lands rather than the turn it charges. The breath attack can poison, confuse or strip badges rather than deal raw damage, so a status-cure item is worth carrying into this fight even if you have not needed one in a while. Being dragged under the stage for a turn is more a tempo loss than a real threat — keep attacking rather than trying to save whoever got grabbed.

sections.name: Guarding and superguarding, frame by frame
sections.card: A regular guard needs the button pressed within about an eighth of a second before a hit lands; get it right and you shave one point of damage off, more with each Damage Dodge badge equipped, and shrug off almost every status effect the attack would have caused. Superguard is the harder version, a much tighter window that blocks the hit completely and hits the attacker back for landing it at all, so it is worth drilling on a weak, predictable enemy before relying on it in a fight that matters. Neither version helps against an item an enemy uses on you, and if an attack targets both Mario and his partner, only the first hit needs a real read: whichever guard you did, or did not do, carries over to the second hit automatically. A few late-game attacks bypass guarding entirely with a lock-out effect that no amount of timing gets around.

sections.name: Boots and Hammer: the upgrade chain
sections.card: Mario's boots and hammer each upgrade twice, and each step is a straight damage jump rather than a new gimmick: a jump attack goes from one damage with the starting Boots to three with the Ultra Boots, and a hammer swing goes from two damage to four with the Super Hammer and six with the Ultra Hammer, all before any attack-boosting badges. Each upgrade also unlocks a field move — the Ultra Boots add a Spring Jump that grabs onto pipes and bars out of normal jumping range, letting you back into areas that looked finished the first time through. The Ultra Hammer can also open a battle with a free first-strike hit at no FP cost, worth using on anything you would rather not spend a turn fighting normally. A later tier always replaces the one before it, so there is no reason to hold onto an earlier hammer or pair of boots once the upgrade is in hand.

sections.name: Monkey bars and swing traversal
sections.card: Monkey bars are horizontal bars the Slayer grabs mid-air and swings along, first taught in Cultist Base and used throughout the campaign to cross gaps, pits and electrified drops. Approach at a run and jump toward the bar rather than at it — grabbing happens automatically once you are close enough in the air, and letting go too early is what causes most falls. Some bars only appear for a short time after a switch, or lower again once you swing off, so cross before double-checking your surroundings. Chaining a bar into a nearby climbable wall or a dash keeps momentum going; stopping mid-swing to aim at an enemy is usually what drops a Slayer into the pit below. If a section has more than one bar in a row, commit to the whole chain rather than pausing between them.

sections.name: The first keycard in Staging Area
sections.card: Doom 64's opening level, Staging Area, hides its first keycard behind a timed switch. Take the elevator up from the starting courtyard and expect enemies to attack from several sides at once on higher skill levels. A switch a short way further on opens a locked door for a limited time, and you need to move quickly to reach it before it shuts — on the easier skill levels the blue key sits out in the open beside that same switch, while on harder settings a berserk pack takes its place there instead. Once you have the blue key, backtrack to the blue door to keep moving through the level. Losing track of which door needs which key is the main way new players get stuck this early, so pick up every key colour you see even before you have found its matching door.

sections.name: How the coloured keycards work
sections.card: Doom 64 uses the same coloured-key system as the rest of the series: a locked door will not open until you are carrying a keycard or skull key of the matching colour, and once picked up a key opens every door of that colour on the level, not just one. Keys are lost the moment you leave a level, so there is no point carrying one forward. Doom 64 goes a step further than the original games: a locked line does not have to be a door at all, it can be any switch or tripwire, and trying to use one without the right key makes your marine grunt while the matching key icon on the status bar flashes so you know exactly which colour you are missing. That flash is the fastest way to work out which key to go back for when a level feels like it has stopped progressing.

sections.name: Finding your way through the dark, maze-like levels
sections.card: Doom 64 is deliberately darker than the games before it, with much of its lighting kept low to build atmosphere, and the North American release ships with its brightness setting at the lowest point on the scale — turning it up in the options menu is the single biggest fix for corridors that look like an unbroken black maze. Beyond that, the layouts reward backtracking rather than a straight line: locked doors and dead ends are normal, and a switch you cannot explain yet usually opens something back the way you came. Listen for the sound of a distant door or switch firing when you press one, since it tells you something changed even if you cannot see where. If a corridor loops back on itself, that is the level working as intended, not a wrong turn — note any unopened coloured door you pass and keep exploring until you find its key.

sections.name: Getting your first star in Bob-omb Battlefield
sections.card: The very first star in Super Mario 64 is Big Bob-omb on the Summit, the first mission of Bob-omb Battlefield. Cross the bridge from the start and follow the path up the mountain, watching for Goombas, wandering Bob-ombs, a Chain Chomp on its post, and iron balls that roll down the spiral road toward you. At the summit you meet the Big Bob-omb himself: walk up to him from the front and he grabs and throws you, so circle around behind him instead, pick him up, and throw him to the ground. Three throws finish the fight. Throwing him off the edge of the summit does not count — he climbs back up, accuses you of cheating, and the fight restarts from the beginning. Once he is beaten the third time, he explodes and leaves behind the Power Star.

sections.name: Crossing Lethal Lava Land without falling in
sections.card: Lethal Lava Land is almost entirely platforms over an open pool of lava, and the Bullies scattered across it are what actually cause most falls, not the jumps themselves — a Bully's whole attack is shoving you backward, and on the narrower platforms that shove goes straight into the lava. Fight them from the middle of a platform rather than its edge, and back them toward a drop instead of letting them back you toward one. The ring platform that circles the volcano briefly stops moving and the volcano erupts with fireballs, so keep moving once it resumes rather than lingering. Inside the volcano itself the platforms get smaller near the top and the jumps are between poles rather than solid ground, so slow down and aim each jump individually. Wearing the Metal Cap before a Bully fight removes the fall risk entirely, since a metal Mario cannot be knocked back by a hit.

sections.name: Picking a kart for top speed
sections.card: Mario Kart 64's eight racers split into three weight classes, and the numbers behind them are fixed: lightweights (Peach, Toad and Yoshi) top out at 314, while every middleweight and heavyweight — Mario, Luigi, D.K., Wario and Bowser alike — caps out lower at 310. Lightweights also accelerate fastest, get the biggest boost from a Mini-Turbo, and lose the least speed driving off-road, which is why they are the pick for outright speed on most courses. The trade-off is handling: they have the widest turning radius of any class and bleed off the most speed in a turn without drifting, and in Battle Mode they spin out from almost any hit, with Toad in particular losing control if anyone bumps him at all. Middleweights turn tightest and are the steadier all-round choice if a course is mostly corners rather than straights.

sections.name: Drifting and Mini-Turbos
sections.card: Mario Kart 64 introduced the Mini-Turbo as a reward for drifting well, and the way to charge one is specific to this game: hop into a drift by holding the drift button through a turn, then rock the control stick left and right while you hold it. Doing that charges a short speed boost that fires the moment you let go of the drift, on top of whatever speed you already had. Later Mario Kart games make this time-based instead, so if you learned to drift on a newer entry the wiggling motion will feel unfamiliar at first — it is deliberate here, not a fluke. The strength of your kart's own handling affects how tightly it drifts, so a kart with worse handling drifts in a wider arc and needs the turn started earlier. Chaining drifts through a series of corners rather than resetting between them keeps you close to top speed for the whole section.

sections.name: Unlocking Extra mode
sections.card: Extra mode — called Mirror Mode in every later Mario Kart game — is the reward for earning gold in all four cups at 150cc, the fastest of the three engine classes. Once unlocked, Extra reuses the same eight courses from 100cc but flips every one of them horizontally, so a corner that used to bend right now bends left and vice versa. The title screen itself changes once Extra is unlocked, which is the easiest way to check whether you actually earned it. The AI in 150cc and Extra leans harder on rubber-banding than the easier classes: expect one or two computer racers to receive a large handicap that lets them recover from being hit and catch back up quickly, so a comfortable lead near the finish line is not as safe as it looks in the two hardest settings.

sections.name: Battle Mode: the four arenas and balloons
sections.card: Battle Mode needs at least two players and puts everyone in an enclosed arena instead of on a racetrack, across four courses: Block Fort, Skyscraper, Double Deck and Big Donut. Every racer starts with three balloons in their own colour, and any item hit or driving off the arena's edge costs one. A heavier character can also pop a lighter one's balloon just by ramming them hard enough — Bowser barrelling into Toad is the extreme case — which is worth remembering when picking a character for this mode rather than for racing. Losing all three balloons turns you into a small, remote-controlled Bomb Kart that can still be attacked and stunned by other players' items, and if it collides with anyone it explodes and you are out for good. The last racer still holding a balloon wins the round.

sections.name: Time Trials and staff ghosts
sections.card: Time Trial mode races you against the clock alone, and after your first clean lap the game saves a ghost of that run for you to chase on your next attempt. The ghost only saves if the run itself was clean — pausing, crashing into an obstacle, driving in reverse, or falling off the track at any point during the lap throws the recording away, so a fast lap with one bad mistake near the end still leaves you with nothing to beat. Three of the eight courses also carry a staff ghost set by the developers, each raced by the character the course is themed around, and those are the only pre-made times in the game — the other five courses have no staff record to chase, only whatever ghost you set yourself.

sections.name: Growing your Pikmin squad
sections.card: Pikmin multiply through their Onion, the hovering hive that matches their colour, and the way to grow a squad is to keep feeding that Onion rather than just picking up loose seeds. Carrying a pellet back to the matching-colour Onion produces new seeds based on the number printed on it, and carrying back a defeated enemy's corpse does the same, usually in far larger numbers than any pellet. If there are fewer Pikmin of that colour in the field than your current limit allows, a returned seed sprouts immediately as a new Pikmin; once you are at the limit, seeds are banked inside the Onion instead and can be called out later, so there is no harm bringing back more than you can use right now. Each colour's Onion is found in a different area rather than all together, so reaching a new area is usually also how you unlock a bigger squad.

sections.name: Throwing Pikmin at enemies and objects
sections.card: Throwing is how you send Pikmin to fight or to work at a distance: aim with the cursor and the game estimates where the Pikmin will land, though a wall or ledge in the way can knock it short of the mark. A thrown Pikmin that hits an enemy mid-flight latches on and starts attacking immediately rather than waiting to land. The next Pikmin in line to be thrown is whichever one is standing closest to your leader, shown on the HUD, so reordering your squad on the ground changes what gets thrown next. Yellow Pikmin fly higher than the rest and reach ledges the others cannot. Purple Pikmin fly faster on a flatter arc and slam down hard enough to stun or knock back whatever they land on, while Rock Pikmin drop on a much lower arc and bounce forward instead of sticking to the spot they land.

sections.name: Classic Mode's Metal Battle
sections.card: Stage 10 of Classic Mode is a one-on-one fight against a metal version of whichever character you are using — every character except Ganondorf, Roy and Mr. Game & Watch can appear this way, and the fight always takes place on Battlefield. Breaking a Metal Box triples a fighter's weight and roughly doubles both fall speed and gravity, so the CPU's metal copy hits the ground fast, cannot recover from an edge as well as it normally could, and is a good target for a vertical juggle or an early edgeguard rather than a horizontal knockout attempt. The weight increase also raises its knockback resistance, so hits that would normally send a fresh copy of that character flying do noticeably less — plan on landing more hits to finish it than the same matchup would normally take, rather than looking for one big kill move.

sections.name: Starting out in Mario Party
sections.card: Turns rotate: each player rolls a 1-10 Dice Block and moves that many spaces, landing on Blue spaces for 3 coins or Red for -3. Passing the Star Space lets you buy a Star for 20 coins if you have enough, and its location shifts to a new random spot each time someone buys one. After everyone moves, a roulette matches players up for that turn's minigame: land all on the same color and everyone plays a 4-player game together, split 2-2 for a team game, or 1 alone against 3 for the odd one out. A new player's biggest surprise is that minigames can take coins from the losers, not just award them to the winner. Games run 20, 35, or 50 turns, and at the end three Bonus Stars go out for the most coins won in minigames, the most coins held, and the most Happening Spaces landed on -- so a last-place player can still close the gap.

sections.name: DK's Jungle Adventure
sections.card: DK's Jungle Adventure is Mario Party's jungle board, built around three Whomps guarding the junctions who each charge 10 coins to let a player through, so early coins go toward paying tolls rather than buying a Star. Landing on a Happening Space sets a boulder rolling down the path near the start, chasing off anyone standing in its way -- worth watching before committing to a route. Bowser also wanders this board and, if you meet him, "rewards" you with a useless Golden Bowser Statue and takes 10 coins for the trouble. Because the Whomps sit on the main junctions, the fastest way to the Star is rarely the free one; budgeting coins for tolls early, rather than saving for a Star purchase, tends to pay off over a full game.

sections.name: Peach's Birthday Cake
sections.card: Peach's Birthday Cake is the smallest board in the original Mario Party, built around Goomba's Flower Lottery: pay 10 coins to plant a red, blue, yellow, or green seed, and the flower that grows either has a Toad face, which points you toward the Star, or a Bowser face, which sends you to buy one of Bowser's bogus items for 20 coins instead. Landing on a Happening Space lets you plant a pricier 30-coin Strawberry Seed that grows into a Piranha Plant; if another player holding Stars later lands on that same Happening Space, the plant steals a Star from them and hands it to whoever planted it. Because the board is small, turns move fast, so the lottery and the strawberry trap end up deciding most games rather than raw movement.

sections.name: Wario's Battle Canyon
sections.card: Wario's Battle Canyon splits into four canyon areas around a central Bowser zone, and players get around by being fired from cannons rather than walking, with a spinning wheel deciding which area you land in next. A Happening Space swaps the direction every cannon fires, which can undo careful planning in a moment. Reaching Bowser's area costs 10 coins paid to a Fly Guy in the northeast, and once there Bowser fires you to a random spot on the board instead of anywhere useful, so it's a detour to avoid unless you're chasing his area for another reason. Because cannon direction can flip at any time, treat this board's routes as unreliable rather than planning several turns ahead.

sections.name: Luigi's Engine Room
