sections.card: Luigi's Engine Room is built around a network of red and blue doors that block or open different paths, switching automatically at the start of every turn, whenever someone lands on certain Happening Spaces, or when a player pays 20 coins to have a robot flip them early. Steam generators near the central engine can be triggered from Happening Spaces to blast a player up to a higher section of the board, often the fastest way past a blocked route. Every path on the board eventually funnels into Warp Pipes near the start, close to Boo, so getting stuck behind a wrong-color door usually costs a lap rather than the whole game. Watching which doors are open before committing to a path matters more here than on most other boards.

sections.name: Mario's Rainbow Castle
sections.card: Mario's Rainbow Castle is a sky board where the Star's location never changes -- it always sits on the main tower -- but every time someone buys a Star, the tower rotates to reveal Bowser instead, who charges 40 coins for a worthless Ztar that wastes coins without affecting anyone's Star count. Any player landing on a Happening Space can also spin the tower early, so the board can flip from Star to Bowser without warning. Because the Star's fixed position makes routing simple, the real skill on this board is timing your approach so you don't arrive right when Bowser is waiting instead.

sections.name: Bowser's Magma Mountain
sections.card: Bowser's Magma Mountain only opens up after every other board has been played once and costs 980 coins to unlock, so it's a late-game board rather than a starting one. Its gimmick is a series of stone heads offering 10-coin shortcuts: accept one and a roulette block decides whether you get the shortcut or are forced back onto the long path. A later purple stone head offers the same gamble for free, but choosing wrong there sends you straight to Bowser, who takes either 20 coins or a Star depending on the roll. Happening Spaces here turn every Blue Space into a Red Space until the board resets, so a run of good luck can turn bad in a single turn.

sections.name: The Mushroom Shop's turn-changing blocks
sections.card: Mario Party's Mushroom Shop sells one-time boosts rather than carried items: a 200-coin Plus Block or 100-coin Minus Block randomly adds or subtracts coins, a Speed Block only rolls 8 to 10 while a Slow Block only rolls 1 to 3, and a Warp Block swaps your position with another player outright. An Event Block instead summons Boo, Koopa Troopa, or Bowser at random. These are bought between games rather than found on the board, so they change your next game rather than the one in progress, and a new player is often surprised that buying one has no effect until the following round starts. The Lucky Box and Casino Box change how your saved coins behave between sessions rather than during a single board game.

sections.name: Mini-Games and Bonus Stars in Mario Party
sections.card: Which kind of minigame you get depends on the color of space everyone lands on: all Blue or all Red spaces gives a 4-player free-for-all, a 2-2 split of colors gives a team game, and one player on the odd color out plays alone against the other three. A Happening Space's color is decided at random before the minigame is picked. Unusually for the series, Mario Party's own minigames can take coins away from the losing side as well as reward the winners, so a bad minigame can cost as much as a bad board turn. At the very end of a game, three Bonus Stars go out for the most coins earned specifically in minigames, the most coins held overall, and the most Happening Spaces landed on, which means a player who never bought a Star can still win outright if they lead in all three categories.

sections.name: Eternal Star and the Baby Bowsers
sections.card: Eternal Star is a bonus board that only opens once you've collected 100 Stars and played every other board at least once, and its gimmick replaces the usual Star Space with seven Baby Bowsers stationed around the board. To take a Star from one, you pay 20 coins and then have to roll higher than the Baby Bowser's own Dice Block -- your roll is capped at 8 to 10, but the Baby Bowser can roll anything, so the odds favor the house. Losing the roll costs you a Star instead of granting one. At the center sits Bowser himself, who takes a Star (or 20 coins if you have none) from anyone who reaches him, sends them back to the start, and scrambles the board's warp routes. A Happening Space here sends everyone back to start too, though it leaves the warp routes as they were.

sections.name: Starting out in Mario Party 2
sections.card: Mario Party 2 keeps the same turn structure as the original -- roll, move, land on a colored space, then play a minigame -- but adds real items for the first time: buy one from an Item Shop, win one from an Item Space's minigame, or hold a Dueling Glove to challenge another player directly for coins. Only one item can be held at a time, unlike later games, so a new player has to decide whether to use an item right away or hold it and risk losing the chance. Bowser Spaces now run a full roulette of bad outcomes rather than a single effect, and a Bank Space lets you deposit coins for another player to potentially collect if they land on it before you pass again. Every board dresses its cast in a costume matching its theme, purely cosmetic but a good sign of which board's rules apply.

sections.name: Pirate Land
sections.card: Pirate Land, the first board, dresses players as pirate captains and uses dock Blue Spaces where a Sushi ferries you to another dock on the board, a fast way to skip ahead if the destination suits you. Happening Spaces trigger a cannon that fires a cannonball at whoever's standing there and sends them straight back to the start, so it's worth checking who's exposed before triggering one. A few shortcuts exist but are guarded by Thwomps who charge a toll starting at one coin, and the fee climbs by a coin every time the next player pays it, so the earliest player through a Thwomp gate always pays the least.

sections.name: Western Land
sections.card: Western Land dresses the cast as cowboys and centers on Steamer, a train that loops the board's perimeter; paying five coins at a toll lets you ride it, and hitting a block afterward decides whether Steamer heads forward or backward. Steamer also moves on its own whenever anyone lands on a Happening Space, and anyone it hits gets sent back to the start, so riders and bystanders both need to track its direction. A milk shop run by Wiggler will, for 20 coins, throw a "hootenanny" that pulls every other character to the shop, which can be used to regroup opponents away from wherever you're headed.

sections.name: Space Land
sections.card: Space Land dresses the cast as astronauts and is built around a Bowser-faced junction in the middle whose countdown ticks down every time someone passes it; when it hits zero, Bowser fires a laser down the board's diagonal path that strips all the coins from anyone caught in it. Happening Spaces send a Whomp or Thwomp chasing whoever landed there, sweeping up any other players in its path along the way. The Snifit Patrol can be paid five coins to set a speed trap that has the Whomp or Thwomp caught by Snifits instead, sending chased players even further away -- a way to turn the board's own hazard against someone else.

sections.name: Mystery Land
sections.card: Mystery Land dresses players as archaeologists and splits the board into four islands that only connect through Happening Spaces, which carry whoever lands on them to the next island clockwise; paying a Bob-omb 10 coins offers a direct shortcut between the upper-left and lower-right islands instead of going the long way around. Shy Guy's Curse House lets a player pay five coins to curse an opponent so their next Dice Block only rolls one to three, a cheap way to slow down whoever's in the lead. Because movement between islands is otherwise limited to Happening Spaces, reaching the right island at the right time matters more here than raw dice luck.

sections.name: Horror Land
sections.card: Horror Land introduces the series' day-and-night cycle: the board starts in daylight and switches every two turns, or whenever a Happening Space is landed on, and paying Kamek 10 coins at the Mystery Mansion flips it to night early. Night changes the map's dangers -- Mr. I charges five coins at night instead of ten during the day to teleport a player (and anyone else in the path) between opposite corners, and the Big Boo in the northeast only appears at night, charging triple the usual fee and stealing from every player at once rather than just one. Whomps here can be paid 10 coins to swap position and open their guarded path, but they stop moving entirely once night falls.

sections.name: Items and the Item Shop in Mario Party 2
sections.card: Mario Party 2 introduced buyable items, sold at Item Shops that change their stock as the game goes on: a Mushroom (10 coins) lets you roll two Dice Blocks and add them together, a Skeleton Key auto-opens locked gates you'd otherwise be stuck behind, and a Dueling Glove (15 coins) summons a Goomba to referee a coin duel against an opponent of your choice. Only one item can be carried at a time. Rarer items only come from Item Mini-Games: a Boo Bell steals coins or a Star for a price, and a Bowser Suit lets you disguise as Bowser and rob 20 coins from anyone you pass. On Bowser Land specifically, a shop run by a Baby Bowser forces whoever passes it to buy an item of his choosing at a markup, unless you're already wearing a Bowser Suit, in which case he gives you a rare item for free.

sections.name: Battle, Item, and Duel Mini-Games
sections.card: Mario Party 2 adds three minigame types beyond the usual 4-player, 2-vs-2, and 1-vs-3 formats. Landing on a Battle Space summons Goomba, who collects a pot of 10 to 50 coins from every player and starts a Battle Mini-Game where first place takes 70% of the pot and second takes the rest, leaving third and fourth with nothing. Item Spaces trigger single-player Item Mini-Games that hand out an item on a win, but only if it isn't the last turn and you don't already hold one. Duel Mini-Games are triggered by using a Dueling Glove rather than by a space, letting a player challenge a specific opponent for a coin wager the two of them agree on beforehand.

sections.name: Bowser Land and the final showdown
sections.card: Bowser Land is Mario Party 2's sixth and final board, unlocked only once every other board has been played at least once, and it flips several of the game's normal rules: passing a bank space here gives you five coins that add to a running loan rather than taking coins away, and landing on that space later means paying the full loan back, losing a Star outright if you can't cover it and have none to spare. Its signature hazard is the Bowser Parade, which starts every five turns and costs two coins per space to anyone caught in its path before sweeping them back to the start; players can redirect the parade's route by paying a Baby Bowser to flip arrow tiles. Whoever places first on this board faces Bowser directly for the game's ending, a tactical coin-and-item board rather than a reflex test.

sections.name: Starting out in Mario Party 3
sections.card: Mario Party 3 keeps the roll-and-move loop from the earlier games but layers on real choices: you can now hold up to three items at once instead of just one, and computer players can be given a handicap to even out a mismatched group. Coins still come from Blue Spaces and go from Red ones, and Happening ("?") Spaces trigger board-specific events. The biggest change for a new player is Duel Mode, played on its own set of boards where two characters fight using partner characters instead of collecting Stars, and Story Mode, a single-player campaign that alternates between normal board games and duels on the way to a set of seven Star Stamps. Party Mode, the game's regular multiplayer format, plays like the earlier two games with these new options layered in.

sections.name: Chilly Waters
sections.card: Chilly Waters is Mario Party 3's ice-themed board, needing 20 coins to buy each Star and centered on an icy five-way junction plus a running Action Time event: landing on a Happening Space in the leftmost column or top row (or paying Mr. Blizzard five coins when you pass him) starts a snowball rolling toward you, and a well-timed button press lets you jump it rather than get chased. If two players are both standing on the frozen lake when the ice cracks, both get swept to a space near the southeast corner and looped back toward the start, which can undo a lot of progress at once. Because the lake and the junction sit in the board's middle, most routes cross through this danger zone rather than around it.

sections.name: Spiny Desert
sections.card: Spiny Desert is Mario Party 3's desert board, and its trick is that there are two Millennium Stars on the board at once -- one real, one a mirage -- with no way to tell them apart until you pass one and it either sells a Star for 20 coins or simply vanishes. Two quicksand pits sit in the upper and lower middle of the board; a Happening Space on either pit's edge pulls in everyone standing around it and spits them out at the other pit instead. A path guarded by two cacti forms the board's Action Time: a well-timed button press gets you past safely, while missing it sends you bouncing off in a random direction. Because the real Star is unmarked, routing here is closer to a guess than a plan.

sections.name: Creepy Cavern
sections.card: Creepy Cavern is Mario Party 3's cave board, and its centerpiece is the Whomp King blocking the only path between the board's upper and lower halves; you can get him to turn around either by handing him a random item as you pass or by landing on a nearby Happening Space, so it's not guaranteed you'll have the right item in hand when you need it. Two horizontal railways can also spawn a minecart from a Happening Space that chases every player on that track to the far end, and paying a Thwomp five coins near the tracks lets you trigger a controlled ride to the other side instead of waiting to be caught. Because the Whomp King sits on the only central crossing, a board where he's turned the wrong way effectively cuts the map in half until someone clears him.

sections.name: Duel Boards and how they work
sections.card: Mario Party 3's Duel Boards, used in both Duel Mode and Story Mode, pit two players against each other using partner characters instead of racing for Stars. Each side starts with five heart segments and one partner, gaining a new partner (chosen semi-randomly, with a "Lucky Roulette" every third lap that slows the wheel down) whenever they pass their own start space. Partners attack automatically when a player passes or lands on the opponent's space, doing damage based on the gap between the attacker's power and the defender's stamina, and each partner also has to be paid a per-turn salary or it walks off the board. A mechanical toy called Belltop sits in the middle of every duel board and, once enough players have passed him, forces both sides into a Duel Mini-Game for double or triple the usual coin stakes.

sections.name: Items and the Item Shop in Mario Party 3
sections.card: Party mode items in Mario Party 3 are sold by two different shopkeepers -- Toad offers helpful items like the Mushroom (roll two dice and add them, 5 coins) and Boo Repellent, while Baby Bowser sells disruptive ones like the Reverse Mushroom, which forces a chosen player's next move to go backward, and the Poison Mushroom, which limits their next roll to one through three. Both shops sell the Skeleton Key, which auto-opens locked gates and can be discarded voluntarily at the start of a turn if you don't need it. You can hold up to three items at once here, unlike the single-item limit in Mario Party 2, and rare items like the Barter Box (swap items with an opponent) or the Koopa Kard (claim an entire bank's savings on the spot) only turn up through Item Spaces, Hidden Blocks, or a purchased Item Bag rather than a normal shop visit.

sections.name: Starting out in Mario Party 6
sections.card: Mario Party 6 keeps the same roll-and-move turns as earlier games but replaces carried items with Orbs, bought from Orb Huts, picked up on Orb Spaces, or won from "?" Spaces; a new player's biggest adjustment is that Orbs, not items, are now the thing worth saving coins for. A day-and-night cycle runs the whole game, switching every three turns and changing which characters host events: Donkey Kong Spaces during the day become Bowser Spaces at night, each running its own set of minigames and rewards. Landing on the same space as another player, or on a Duel Space, triggers a Duel Mini-Game with a bet of coins, a Star, or both riding on the result -- a bigger risk than the coin-only duels of earlier games.

sections.name: Towering Treetop
sections.card: Towering Treetop is Mario Party 6's treehouse-themed board, and its main twist is that the Star Space itself moves to a new random spot every time someone buys a Star, so there's no fixed destination to plan a route toward the way there is on some other boards. The paths through the trees also change length depending on whether it's day or night, which can make a shortcut from an earlier turn disappear or reappear. Because the target keeps relocating, players tend to buy Orbs that speed up movement or warp them across the board rather than Orbs that only help with a single fixed route.

sections.name: E. Gadd's Garage
sections.card: E. Gadd's Garage shares Towering Treetop's moving Star Space, but wraps it in Professor E. Gadd's workshop full of gadgets and machinery whose paths also shift between day and night. Because two of the board's defining features -- the relocating Star and the changing paths -- both depend on timing rather than positioning, a new player's instinct to head straight toward the Star works less well here than tracking which route is currently open and buying Orbs (like the board-specific Bullet Bill Orb, which lets you overtake an opponent and steal 20 coins) that fit whichever layout is active.

sections.name: Snowflake Lake
sections.card: Snowflake Lake changes the whole goal: every player starts the board already holding five Stars, and the only way to get more is by riding a Chain Chomp to steal them from an opponent, rather than buying them from a Star Space at all. This flips the normal Mario Party incentive to avoid losing Stars into an incentive to actively hunt other players down, and a lead built early can evaporate in one Chain Chomp ride near the end. Because Snack Orbs exist elsewhere in the series specifically to block a Chain Chomp theft for a few turns, holding a defensive Orb matters more on this board than almost anywhere else.

sections.name: Castaway Bay
sections.card: Castaway Bay is a mostly linear tropical board where the Star is purchased from Donkey Kong waiting at the far end, rather than from a fixed Star Space along the path. Bowser periodically swaps in for Donkey Kong at that same spot, and reaching him instead costs you a Star outright, or 20 coins if you don't have one to lose -- so timing your arrival, not just your speed, decides whether the trip pays off. Because the board is largely a single track rather than a branching map, positioning to arrive right after Bowser swaps back out for Donkey Kong is the board's main skill.

sections.name: Orbs in Mario Party 6
sections.card: Orbs replace the carried items of the first three games and come in color-coded families: green Self Orbs like the Mushroom (move with two Dice Blocks, 5 coins) or Metal Mushroom (immune to rivals' traps) affect only the player who uses them, while red Orbs are set as traps on a space and trigger only when someone else passes or lands there, after which they vanish. A handful of Orbs are board-specific rather than universal -- the Flutter Orb, which flies you straight to the Star Space, is only sold on Towering Treetop and E. Gadd's Garage, and the Warp Pipe Orb only appears on three of the six boards -- so what's worth saving coins for changes depending on which board you're playing.

sections.name: Mini-game types and Mic Mode
sections.card: Which minigame plays depends on the color of space everyone landed on, same as earlier games, but Mario Party 6 adds Mic minigames that use the packaged GameCube microphone for voice commands, playable if the Mic setting is turned on. Battle minigames still happen at random with a shared coin pot, but here players vote for which minigame they want rather than leaving the choice to a roulette wheel. Duel minigames trigger from Duel Spaces or from two players landing on the same space during the last five turns, and DK or Bowser minigames only appear when a player lands on their respective board space, with the active host -- Donkey Kong by day, Bowser by night -- changing which of the two can trigger at all.

sections.name: Clockwork Castle, the final board
sections.card: Clockwork Castle is Mario Party 6's final board, bought with 100 Stars from the Star Bank rather than unlocked through normal play, and it turns the day-and-night cycle into the whole challenge: by day, players chase Donkey Kong around the gear-covered board for a Star, and he always rolls and moves after everyone else has finished their turn, moving twice if he eats a banana along the way. By night, the goal flips to avoiding Bowser instead, who has reversed the board's direction and also moves twice if he breathes fire; getting caught by him costs a Star, or 20 coins if you're holding none. Because the chase-or-avoid goal swaps with the time of day, tracking the day/night meter matters as much as tracking your own position on the board.

genre_patterns.card: Soulslike basics: learn dodge timing, stamina management, and safe heal windows. Summon allies when available; upgrade vigor before glass-cannon damage.
